name: Positivity Effect
description: Older adults often attend to and remember positive information relatively more than negative information, compared with younger adults. This is a specific aging-and-emotion-regulation finding, not a generic optimism claim.
design_relevance_note: Relevant to older-adult UX, health communication, reminder framing, memory supports, and emotionally charged interfaces. Age-targeted products may not get the same balance of attention and memory from negative framing that younger-user research suggests.
prevalence_note: Specialized terminology mainly relevant in aging, healthcare, and accessibility-oriented design work rather than mainstream day-to-day product review.

findings.description: A meta-analysis found a reliable age-related positivity effect: compared with younger adults, older adults preferentially attend to and remember positive over negative information. The effect is real on average but moderated by task and context rather than being an all-purpose positivity bias.
findings.source_title: Meta-analysis of the age-related positivity effect: Age differences in preferences for positive over negative information.
